Operator: Good morning, and welcome to the Apex Insurance Group Third Quarter 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. [Operator Instructions] As a reminder, this conference is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Sarah Thompson, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Thompson: Thank you, Operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to Apex Insurance Group's Third Quarter 2024 earnings call. Joining me on the call today are John Reynolds, Chief Executive Officer; Michael Chen, Chief Financial Officer; Lisa Patel, Chief Underwriting Officer; David Kim, Chief Investment Officer; and Emily Vargas, Chief Operating Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that some of the statements we are making today may be considered forward-looking. These statements are subject to certain risks and uncertainties that could cause our actual results to differ materially from those projected. We encourage you to review our SEC filings for a more detailed discussion of these risks and uncertainties.

I will now turn the call over to John Reynolds.

John Reynolds: Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us today. I'm pleased to report on Apex Insurance Group's performance for the third quarter. We delivered strong results, driven by robust gross written premiums growth across our lines of business, solid realized and unrealized gains on investments, reliable reinsurance recoveries, disciplined management of catastrophe losses, the positive impact of our pricing changes on premium volume, and thoughtful capital deployment plans including acquisitions and new products. We are particularly excited about the initial success of our ApexDrive telematics program and its meaningful improvement in loss ratios through usage-based pricing.

Michael, our CFO, will now provide a more detailed review of our financial performance.

Michael Chen: Thank you, John. Good morning, everyone. As John mentioned, we had a solid quarter. Our net income was $612 million, or $2.10 per share. Key drivers of our financial performance included strong top-line growth, favorable investment returns, reinsurance support, controlled catastrophe impacts, pricing discipline, and strategic capital allocation. Our combined ratio was 93.2%. Investment income for the quarter was $412 million, reflecting strong performance in our fixed income and alternatives segments. We continue to maintain a strong capital position, with a group-wide RBC ratio of 512%.

Let me now turn to our top-line performance, where we delivered another quarter of robust Gross Written Premiums—or GWP—growth, up 9.2% year-over-year to $14.8 billion in Q3. This marks our 11th consecutive quarter of double-digit organic growth in many core lines, driven by a combination of disciplined pricing, strong retention above 91% across the portfolio, and new business wins totaling $1.2 billion—up 15% from last year.

Let me break this down by line of business, as we always do, to give you visibility into the drivers and our strategic positioning. I'll highlight year-over-year GWP growth percentages, rate changes, retention trends, and key initiatives. All figures exclude the impact of our recent acquisition of Midwest Casualty, which added about 2 points to overall growth.

Personal Lines continues to be our growth engine, representing 41% of total GWP, with +7.8% GWP growth to $6.1 billion. Auto premiums grew 6.5%, reflecting a 4.2% average rate increase amid persistent repair inflation—now running at 12% annually per CCC Intelligent Solutions data—and higher claims frequency from distracted driving trends. Our telematics program, ApexDrive, now penetrates 28% of our policies, delivering a 15% loss ratio improvement through usage-based pricing. Retention held steady at 92.5%, with new business up 8% thanks to our partnership with enhancements inspired by Progressive's Snapshot model.

Homeowners and Dwelling Fire surged 10.1%, fueled by 7.8% rate hikes in catastrophe-exposed states like Florida and California, where reinsurance costs stabilized post-Hurricane Ian. Exposure growth was modest at 2%, but our parametric reinsurance structures with Swiss Re capped tail risks, allowing us to maintain availability in high-hazard zones. Wildfire mitigation credits via our ApexGuard app—adopted by 150,000 policyholders—boosted multi-line attachment by 3 points.

Commercial Lines was the standout, +12.4% GWP growth to $5.9 billion, up sharply on mid-single-digit rate momentum and market share gains. Small Commercial—our bread-and-butter segment under $5 million premium size—grew 11.2%, with rates up 5.9% and retention at a stellar 93.8%. We captured 4 points of share in the middle market via our AI-powered underwriting platform, which reduced cycle times by 40% and improved quote conversion to 65%. Key wins included expanding our Business Owners Policy (BOP) suite with embedded cyber coverage, resonating amid rising ransomware attacks—up 30% per Chainalysis reports.

Workers' Compensation jumped 14.7%, our fastest grower, benefiting from 8.2% rate increases and a 22% ramp in new business from construction and logistics sectors. Our partnership with Verisk's ISO rating tools and claims predictive analytics kept the loss ratio at 68%, well below the industry average of 75%. Middle-market Property grew 13.1%, though we selectively withdrew from high-cat exposures in Texas petrochemicals, prioritizing profitability over volume.

Specialty Lines rounded out the quarter with +15.6% GWP growth to $2.4 billion, with tailwinds from capacity constraints in a hardening market. Directors & Officers (D&O) premiums rose 18.2%, with rates firming 12% on litigation risks tied to ESG disclosures and SEC scrutiny—echoing trends seen at peers like Chubb and AIG. Our quota share with Berkshire Hathaway reinsurance provided the firepower for 25% new business growth here.

Cyber insurance exploded 22.4%, now 10% of Specialty GWP, as clients flocked to our modular product amid a 50% YoY rise in incidents per CrowdStrike's 2023 report. We deployed parametric cyber triggers for rapid payouts, differentiating us from Travelers and Hartford. Environmental and Trade Credit lines grew 11%, supported by our expansion into Asia-Pacific renewables.

Geographically, U.S. operations drove 72% of growth at +10.1%, led by Southeast rate relief post-storms. Europe added +6.8% on Motor and Liability, tempered by softer UK pricing but offset by German commercial wins via our Lloyd's syndicate. APAC contributed +14.2%, with India auto up 20% through our tie-up with HDFC Ergo, and Australia Property gaining from flood reinsurance resets. Emerging markets now represent 8% of GWP, up from 5% two years ago.

This GWP trajectory underscores our "Profitable Growth 2.0" strategy: data-led pricing via our proprietary CatIQ model, which incorporates climate risk scenarios out to 2030; digital distribution partnerships yielding 30% cheaper acquisition costs; and reinsurance optimization—our Q3 ceded premium ratio fell to 28% from 32%, bolstering the balance sheet.

Looking forward, we expect full-year GWP growth of 9-11%, with Q4 acceleration in Commercial and Specialty. Rate momentum should sustain at 5-7% into 2024, though we'll monitor inflation and cat activity closely—our all-peril nat cat budget is $1.1 billion. Combined ratio guidance remains 92-94%, supporting EPS growth of 12%.

Before moving on, I'd like to dive deep into our investment performance, specifically realized and unrealized gains and losses, which contributed a net $187 million to our bottom line this quarter—up 24% from Q3 2023. As you know, our $162 billion general account investment portfolio is the engine that powers our insurance operations, generating spread income to support our Property & Casualty (P&C) and Life & Annuity businesses. We maintain a conservative, liability-driven asset allocation with a book yield of 4.2%, duration of 5.8 years closely matched to our ALM targets, and a high-quality tilt—72% investment-grade fixed maturities, 12% equities, 8% structured securities like RMBS and CLOs, and 8% alternatives including direct lending and infrastructure.

Our realized gains came in strong at $312 million pre-tax, a 15% YoY increase, driven primarily by tactical sales in our fixed income and equity sleeves. In fixed maturities—which make up the lion's share—we realized $185 million in gains from pruning $4.2 billion notional of legacy positions. Specifically, we sold intermediate corporates where spreads had tightened 25 bps quarter-over-quarter, locking in gains from purchases made in the 2022-2023 rate-hike cycle when 10-year Treasury yields bottomed at 3.8%. Think names like investment-grade issuers in energy transition plays—similar to what we've seen peers like Chubb and Travelers capitalize on.

On the equity side, $98 million in realizations stemmed from our $19 billion common stock portfolio, where we trimmed 2% of overweight positions in financials and tech, including selective sales in regional banks post their Q2 stress tests and a rotation out of mega-caps like the Magnificent Seven amid valuation concerns. Our alternatives bucket added $29 million, mainly from harvesting returns in a $3.5 billion direct lending fund yielding 8.2% net—outperforming benchmarks like the Cliffwater Direct Lending Index by 150 bps.

Offsetting these were $20 million in realized losses from credit-impaired names—a single-name corporate default in the commercial real estate sector, echoing broader CRE headwinds we've all been watching. But our credit monitoring—powered by our proprietary AI-driven early-warning system, which flags 15% more potential downgrades than traditional models—allowed us to exit early, limiting OTTI charges to under 0.1% of the portfolio.

Unrealized marks showed a $125 million net loss, or 8 bps drag on portfolio NAV, entirely in AOCI under our AFS accounting. This was dominated by fixed income, with a $1.1 billion unrealized loss on our $116 billion bond portfolio due to the yield curve's bear steepening—10-year swaps up 18 bps to 4.15%, 30-year to 4.35%. Duration extension from our modest barbell strategy amplified this by about 10%, but it's largely a paper loss; our liability durations are matched within 0.3 years, so no meaningful economic P&L hit.

Regionally, U.S. Treasuries and agencies drove 55% of the mark-downs as Fed pause rhetoric gave way to hotter-than-expected CPI prints. European sovereigns added $220 million in losses amid ECB rate cut delays and widening German Bund spreads. Positively, our $8 billion emerging markets sleeve—tilted to Asia ex-Japan investment-grades like Korean industrials—posted $45 million in unrealized gains as local yields compressed on stronger growth outlooks.

Equities contributed a $65 million unrealized gain, fueled by the S&P 500's 5% Q3 rally, though we saw volatility in our 20% allocation to dividend aristocrats. Alternatives were flat, with infrastructure funds like those mirroring Brookfield's model gaining on renewable energy tailwinds.

YoY, unrealized losses narrowed 40% from the $2.1 billion trough in Q4 2022, reflecting our active duration management—we shortened by 0.4 years via $2.8 billion in pay-fixed swaps during the March Fed pivot. This positions us better than peers like Progressive, whose longer durations have saddled them with persistent AOCI holes.

Portfolio-wise, new money yields rose to 5.1%—our highest in a decade—from deploying $6.5 billion in premiums into 5-7% CLO equity tranches and private credit, capitalizing on dislocated spreads post-bank failures. We're targeting a 50 bps spread compression in 2025 via sector rotation into munis and ABS, where we see value amid fiscal deficits.

Technically, we've rolled out our next-gen ALM platform with BlackRock's Aladdin integration, incorporating climate risk scenarios that dynamically adjust for 2-degree warming pathways—reducing tail VaR by 12%. ESG is now 28% of the portfolio, with $12 billion in green bonds yielding 4.8%, outperforming vanillas by 20 bps.

Regionally, North America remains 65% of AUM, but we're growing APAC exposure to 15% via annuity sales in Japan, hedging FX with JPY forwards. In Europe, post-Brexit regulatory tailwinds let us boost UK gilts, which gained 3% unrealized on BoE signals.

Looking forward, with two cuts penciled in by year-end, we expect $400-500 million in realizations next year from equity trims and bond roll-downs, while unrealized losses stabilize as rates mean-revert. Our ROA spread target of 120 bps remains on track, supporting 10% EPS growth.

This disciplined approach—blending income stability with opportunistic realizations—underscores why our investment ROE of 7.2% leads P&C peers.

Next, I'd like to spend a few minutes on our reinsurance recoveries received and expected, as this continues to be a key driver of our earnings stability and loss ratio performance in what has been an extraordinarily active catastrophe year. As you know, our reinsurance program is structured to protect against tail risks, with a diversified panel including leaders like Swiss Re, Munich Re, RenaissanceRe, and emerging capacity from Lloyd's syndicates. We've maintained a robust 40% quota share on our U.S. property cat book and excess-of-loss layers starting at $100 million per occurrence, which has proven resilient amid the hardening reinsurance market.

In Q3 2024, we recognized $285 million in reinsurance recoveries received, up 42% from the $200 million in Q3 2023 and 15% ahead of our initial guidance of $248 million. Year-to-date through September 30, cumulative recoveries stand at $612 million, representing a recovery rate of 87% against our gross incurred losses of $704 million YTD. This outperformance was driven primarily by accelerated cash collections on prior-year catastrophe events, particularly Hurricane Idalia from Q3 2023 and the California wildfires in Q4 2023. For context, our cash recovery timing has improved markedly—average collection lag is now down to 4.5 months from 6.2 months a year ago—thanks to proactive claims advocacy and streamlined arbitration clauses we negotiated during our January 2024 treaty renewals.

Breaking it down by line of business, property and casualty, which accounts for 72% of our ceded premiums, delivered $210 million in Q3 recoveries, or 91% of gross cat losses in that segment. This reflects our facultative placements with PartnerRe on high-severity windstorm risks, where we've recovered 95% of ceded losses to date. In contrast, our liability lines saw $45 million in recoveries, slightly below expectations at 78% recovery rate, due to ongoing disputes on a few large U.S. bodily injury claims from the 2022 Florida floods. Life and health contributed the balance at $30 million, steady quarter-over-quarter, supported by our stop-loss treaties with Hannover Re.

Regionally, North America dominated with $220 million, or 77% of Q3 total, fueled by $150 million from U.S. Southeast hurricanes—think Ian remnants and early-season Tropical Storm Alberto. Our modeling with RMS v17.1 has allowed us to validate these claims swiftly, minimizing IBNR adjustments. Europe chipped in $40 million, primarily from German floods echoing last summer's events, where we've secured 85% recoveries under our pan-European excess-of-loss tower with SCOR. Asia-Pacific was lighter at $25 million, impacted by slower remittances from Japanese typhoon claims, but we're expecting a catch-up in Q4 as our Tokyo-based adjusters finalize assessments.

Looking ahead to expected recoveries, we now guide to $950 million to $1.05 billion for full-year 2024, up from our prior range of $850 million to $950 million. This incorporates $180 million in near-term cash expectations for Q4 from open 2023/2024 cat positions, plus $250 million in ultimate recoverables booked as of September 30. Key tailwinds include favorable development on our 2022 accident year reserve, where we've released $45 million in adverse prior-year development offsets through better-than-expected reinsurance billing. However, we remain vigilant on risks: potential commutations with underperforming quota share partners could shave 5-7% off expectations, and escalating reinflation on construction claims in Australia might pressure our workers' comp recoveries.

Strategically, we're not resting on these results. We've launched a technical initiative called 'ReinsureOptix,' our proprietary AI-driven platform integrating Verisk catastrophe models and blockchain for immutable claims tracking. This has reduced disputes by 30% YTD and accelerated recoveries by embedding smart contract triggers for automatic payouts on verified losses exceeding $50 million. At renewal, we shifted 10% of our cat capacity to collateralized ILS funds like Stone Ridge and Fermat, locking in fixed pricing amid 25% rate hikes industry-wide—far outpacing the 8% gross premium growth we saw on our primary book.

On the market front, the reinsurance cycle remains firm, with January 2024 renewals seeing property cat rates up 20-30% per Swiss Re's sigma report, but alternative risk transfer is getting pricier due to high interest rates squeezing cat bond spreads to 450 bps. We're countering this by optimizing our attachment points—raising the primary layer deductible by 15% on non-U.S. perils—and exploring parametric triggers for flood risks in the UK and Benelux, partnering with Descartes Underwriting.

In summary, our reinsurance recoveries underscore the strength of our program: high recovery rates bolstering our net loss ratio to 62.4% in Q3, down 210 basis points year-over-year, and contributing 18% to our operating EPS of $2.10. This positions us well for combined ratio convergence toward our 95% target, even as cat activity persists. We're confident in delivering mid-teens ROE through the cycle.

As we dive further into the financials, I'd like to address one of our most closely watched metrics: total catastrophe losses impact, both in absolute USD terms and as a percentage of gross written premium, or GWP. This is a critical lens for understanding our property and casualty, or P&C, underwriting performance amid a year that's seen elevated nat cat activity globally.

For the quarter ended September 30, 2024, our total catastrophe losses net of reinsurance recoveries came in at $1.45 billion, representing 9.2% of our quarterly GWP of $15.8 billion. This compares to $850 million, or 5.8% of GWP, in Q3 2023, and $1.1 billion, or 7.4% of GWP, in Q2 2024. Year-to-date through Q3, cumulative cat losses stand at $3.7 billion, or 8.1% of YTD GWP of $45.6 billion—up from 6.2% in the prior-year period. These figures are reported on an ultimate basis, incorporating our latest IBNR reserves and third-party actuarial reviews.

To give you the full picture, let's break this down by key drivers. The quarter's losses were dominated by U.S. Southeast windstorm events, particularly Hurricane Lila—a Category 4 storm making landfall in Florida with estimated industry losses north of $60 billion, per RMS modeling. Our gross exposure there triggered $950 million in paid and reserved losses across our homeowners, commercial multi-peril, and auto physical damage lines, with a net impact of $620 million after ceding 65% to our quota share and excess-of-loss reinsurance towers. This pushed our U.S. P&C cat loss ratio to 28% for the quarter, well above our long-term target of 12-15%.

Regionally, we also saw $280 million from European floods in Germany and Poland—reminiscent of the 2021 Ahr Valley events but more contained due to improved river modeling—netting $180 million post-reinsurance. In APAC, Australian bushfires contributed $210 million gross, or $140 million net, driven by our growing workers' comp and liability books in high-exposure states like New South Wales. Latin America added $110 million from Mexican earthquakes, a smaller but volatile contributor given our 15% market share in facultative reinsurance there.

Excluding cats, our attritional loss ratio remained disciplined at 52%, helping deliver a calendar-year combined ratio of 102.4%—in line with peers like Chubb and Travelers, who reported similar pressures. But let's be clear: these cat losses shaved 140 points off our underlying combined ratio, underscoring the volatility we're navigating.

On trends, we're seeing a multi-year uptick driven by climate-amplified frequency and severity. Per our internal cat bond analytics and Verisk Analytics data, 1-in-100-year events are now occurring every 2-3 years in key perils. Our probable maximum loss, or PML, for a 1-in-250-year U.S. hurricane has risen 18% YoY to $4.2 billion gross, reflecting portfolio growth in Florida and Texas homeowners—up 12% in premium terms. Globally, cat losses as % of GWP have trended from 4.5% in 2021 to 7.8% YTD 2024 across the industry, per AM Best aggregates.

Strategically, we're not standing still. We've launched Atlas CatShield 2.0, our AI-enhanced catastrophe modeling platform, integrating satellite imagery from Planet Labs, climate projections from NOAA, and machine learning for dynamic PML simulations. This has improved our pricing accuracy by 22%, allowing us to index catastrophe loadings in 65% of our U.S. commercial renewals—similar to how Swiss Re has deployed their own Sigma models. We've also optimized our reinsurance program: our $2.5 billion cat XOL tower now features parametric triggers for wind and flood, reducing tail risk by 15 bps on economic capital, and we've issued $400 million in cat bonds via our Irish SPV, targeting ILS investors at a 6.5% coupon.

Regionally, we're de-risking high-hazard zones: U.S. gross exposure down 8% via non-renewals in California wildfire zones, offset by 20% growth in low-cat Midwest agribusiness. In Europe, we're partnering with AXA XL on index-based covers for flood reinsurance, capping our net retention at 2% of GWP. Looking forward, we expect Q4 cat losses at 6-8% of GWP, assuming no major U.S. landfallers beyond the active Atlantic season forecast. Full-year guidance holds at 7.5-8.5% of GWP, with ROE targeting 12% post-cats.

This positions us well for 2025 rate cycles, where we're projecting 5-7% hardening in U.S. P&C amid capacity constraints. Our balance sheet remains fortress-like with a 250% RBC ratio, giving us flexibility to recycle cat recoveries into share buybacks or bolt-on M&A in cyber and specialty lines, which saw zero cat impact this quarter.

Before we open for questions, I'd like to dive deeper into one of the key drivers behind our top-line performance: the impact of our pricing changes on premium volume. As you know, in a hardening Property & Casualty (P&C) market characterized by persistent inflation in auto repair costs, medical expenses, and reinsurance treaty renewals, we've maintained a disciplined pricing strategy to protect our margins while driving sustainable growth.

First, a high-level snapshot: For Q3, our consolidated Gross Written Premium (GWP) grew 7.2% year-over-year to $14.8 billion, with Net Premiums Written (NPW) up 6.9% to $12.6 billion. This marks the sixth consecutive quarter of double-digit underlying premium growth when adjusted for foreign exchange and prior-year development. Pricing was the primary engine here, contributing approximately 65% of that growth, or about 470 basis points, with the balance from higher submission volumes and improved retention.

In Personal Lines, which represents 55% of our book, we saw robust premium expansion despite moderating rate momentum. Personal Auto premiums grew 9.1% YoY to $5.2 billion in NPW. We executed average earned rate increases of 10.2% across the portfolio—up from 9.8% in Q2—targeting states with elevated loss trends like California and Florida, where bodily injury claim severity has surged 15% due to litigated soft tissue claims and social inflation. This pricing discipline offset a 2% decline in policies-in-force (PIF) from non-renewals in high-risk coastal zones, yielding net volume growth. Homeowners and Other Personal Lines added another 8.4% premium growth to $3.1 billion NPW, driven by 7.5% average rate hikes amid rebuilding cost inflation (now at 12% YoY per CoreLogic data) and increased wind/hail deductibles. Notably, our telematics penetration reached 28% in Auto—up from 22% a year ago—allowing granular pricing via usage-based insurance (UBI) models, which improved loss picks by 4 points and boosted retention to 87.5%, versus the industry average of 84% per JD Power.

Shifting to Commercial Lines, 40% of our mix, premium volume accelerated to 11.3% YoY growth, with NPW hitting $4.9 billion—the strongest quarter since Q4 2022. Here, pricing changes were more aggressive: average rate increases of 12.8% across middle-market and large accounts, compared to 11.5% in Q2. This was fueled by a 6% rise in the AM Best Commercial Composite Rate Index and our own exposure management in catastrophe-prone classes like habitational real estate. Workers' Compensation saw 14.2% premium growth on 9.8% rates, countering a 5% payroll shrinkage in construction-exposed accounts. General Liability and Umbrella lines benefited from our AI-driven pricing engine, UnityPrice 3.0, which incorporates real-time loss cost monitoring from Verisk Analytics and third-party data lakes. This tech initiative segmented risks more precisely, reducing adverse selection by 3 points and enabling 15% new business flow growth. Retention held steady at 89%, outpacing peers like Travelers (87%) and Chubb (88%), thanks to multi-year deal structures with embedded escalators tied to CPI.

Regionally, the U.S. drove 72% of our premium growth, with 8.5% NPW expansion to $9.1 billion. California Personal Lines premiums rose 12% despite regulatory scrutiny under Prop 103, where we layered in 11.5% pure premium adjustments via independent rate filings approved by the CDI. Florida's book grew 6% post-Hurricane Idalia recon, with 14% rates and a shift to higher-layer reinsurance via our 1/1 renewal at a 25% cost increase—mitigating net retentions. In contrast, our EMEA operations faced softer market dynamics, with UK Motor premiums flat at £1.2 billion equivalent amid the FCA's pricing remedies, but we offset this with 7% Commercial rates in Germany and Benelux, leveraging EU Solvency II capital efficiencies for selective growth. Asia-Pacific contributed 4% growth to $1.4 billion NPW, led by 10% Auto rates in Australia amid rising third-party liability costs, though Japan tempered to 3% due to yen depreciation.

Now, on elasticity and trade-offs: Our pricing actions have been measured to balance volume and profitability. Elasticity analysis from our actuarial team shows a -0.6 price sensitivity coefficient in Personal Auto—meaning a 10% rate increase typically yields a 6% volume drop, which we've contained to 4% through competitive positioning against direct writers like Progressive and Geico. This preserved our Personal Lines ex-cat combined ratio at 95.2%, down 120 bps YoY. Technically, we've invested $150 million YTD in pricing sophistication: rolling out machine learning models trained on 500 million+ claims records for hyper-local ratemaking, integrating satellite imagery for property perils via Planet Labs data, and dynamic pricing APIs for broker portals. These have improved rate adequacy by 2.5 points, directly supporting premium momentum without eroding book quality.

Strategically, this positions us well in a market transitioning from hard to plateauing cycles. Reinsurance costs stabilized at our July 1 renewal, with a blended ceded rate of +18% versus +32% last year, freeing capacity for growth. We're targeting 8-10% premium growth in FY24, with pricing contributing 5-7 points, while monitoring macro risks like Fed rate cuts potentially softening Commercial renewals. Our dividend-adjusted book value per share grew 11% this quarter, underscoring the flywheel effect of pricing-led growth on returns.

In summary, our pricing changes have not just defended margins but catalyzed premium volume expansion in a claims-intensive environment. We're proud of the execution and remain committed to underwriting discipline.

As we wrap up our Q3 results, I'd like to outline our capital deployment strategy, which remains a cornerstone of delivering superior shareholder value in this dynamic insurance landscape. At Apex Global, we ended the quarter with a robust capital position: consolidated shareholders' equity of $28.4 billion, up 8% year-over-year, and a group-wide RBC ratio of 512%, well above our 400% target operating range. This gives us approximately $4.2 billion in deployable excess capital over the next 12-18 months, based on our stress-tested SST (Swiss Solvency Test) and ORSA projections, factoring in potential nat cat escalations from climate volatility.

Our deployment philosophy is disciplined and opportunistic: prioritizing high-return organic growth, bolt-on M&A in high-growth adjacencies, product innovation to capture embedded value, and consistent shareholder returns. We target a mid-teens ROE through the cycle, and we're on track with a 14.2% trailing 12-month ROE, supported by our attritional combined ratio of 92.4% ex-cat.

First, on acquisitions. We've been active but selective, focusing on tuck-in deals that enhance our P&C and specialty lines while bolstering our digital capabilities. In Q2, we closed the $1.1 billion acquisition of Nordic Re's commercial P&C book in the Nordics and Baltics—a portfolio with $650 million in annualized gross written premiums (GWP), a pristine 88% combined ratio, and strong motor and liability exposures. This not only adds 2 points to our EPS accretion in year one but positions us to cross-sell our cyber and D&O products into a region where cyber claims have surged 35% YoY per EIOPA data. Integration is 75% complete, with $45 million in synergies already realized through back-office consolidation on our Salesforce-based policy admin system.

Looking ahead, we're advancing discussions on two fronts. In the U.S., we're eyeing a $750 million bid for a mid-tier insurtech like a scaled-down version of Hippo or Root, targeting homeowners in catastrophe-prone Southeast markets. This would bring parametric trigger tech for hurricane deductibles, aligning with rising secondary perils—think $150 billion in insured losses from 2024 U.S. wild weather per Swiss Re sigma. Internationally, we're in exclusivity for a 51% stake in an Asia-Pacific health micro-insurer with $400 million GWP, focused on parametric hospital indemnity products. APAC represents 22% of our book now, up from 18% in 2023, driven by 12% GWP growth amid India's IRDAI liberalization and Southeast Asia's gig economy boom. We'd fund this via a mix of cash ($300 million) and $150 million in mandatory convertible notes at 4.5% coupon, preserving our A+ AM Best rating.

Shifting to new products and organic innovation. We're allocating $800 million—or 19% of deployable capital—to R&D and launches, emphasizing tech-enabled lines where loss ratios are sub-60% and margins exceed 25%. Key initiatives include:

Cyber insurance expansion: Launching "Apex CyberShield Pro" in Q4, a usage-based policy with AI-driven risk scoring via our proprietary Sentinel platform (powered by Google Cloud ML). Initial GWP target: $500 million in 2025, pricing at $15k per $10M limit—competitive with Chubb's Cyber ERM but with 20% faster quoting via API integrations. This taps a $15 billion global market growing at 25% CAGR, per McKinsey, amid ransomware payouts hitting $1.1 billion in Q3 alone (per Chainalysis).

Climate-resilient parametric products: Building on our Bermuda hull book, we're rolling out "StormGuard Index" for APAC agriculture—triggering payouts based on satellite-derived wind speed and yield data from partners like Gro Intelligence. $200 million pilot GWP in 2025, with 35% margins post-reinsurance via RenaissanceRe towers. This counters basis risk criticisms leveled at traditional indemnity, especially with El Niño fading into La Niña patterns per NOAA.

Embedded insurance via B2B2C: $150 million investment in white-label APIs for e-commerce platforms, mimicking Allianz's embedX model. Targeting 15% attachment rates on auto and travel trips, with telematics from our Cambridge Mobile app feeding dynamic pricing. Early traction: 28% conversion in U.S. pilots with Uber Eats partners.

Regionally, North America (55% of GWP) remains our growth engine at 9% YoY, fueled by commercial lines hardening post-IFRS 17 transition. Europe (25%) is stabilizing post-Ukraine nat cats, with our £300 million Solace Re cat bond issuance covering 1-in-200-year floods. APAC and LatAm (20% combined) are the stars, with 15%+ growth from bancassurance tie-ups like our ICICI Lombard JV in India.

Finally, shareholder returns. To balance growth, we're committing $1.5 billion to buybacks and dividends. Q3 dividend up 10% to $0.72/share, yielding 2.8% forward. And we've authorized a $1 billion open-market repurchase, with 4% velocity targeting our $85 intrinsic value per NAV (per analyst consensus). This leaves dry powder for opportunistic M&A if pricing softens—we're monitoring dislocated assets like Evergrande-linked China exposures.

In summary, our capital plan is about compounding value: 60% growth/M&A, 20% innovation, 20% returns. We're conviction-weighted toward specialty risks where we have moats in data and distribution.

Lisa Patel: Thank you, Michael. I'd like to provide an update on our underwriting performance. We've seen continued strong performance in our Commercial Lines business. We are actively managing our exposure to catastrophe risks and have implemented several initiatives to improve our risk selection, including AI-powered underwriting platforms and advanced catastrophe modeling.

David Kim: Thank you. From an investment perspective, we have continued to focus on diversifying our portfolio and managing risk in the current market environment. We are seeing positive returns from our investments in structured securities and alternatives.

Operator, we are now ready to open the line for questions.

Operator: Thank you. [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from Alex Rivera with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

Alex Rivera: Good morning. Can you provide more color on the GWP growth by line of business, particularly in Specialty?

Operator: Our next question comes from Jordan Lee with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

Jordan Lee: Good morning. Could you discuss the impact of inflation on your business?

Michael Chen: Good morning, Jordan. Inflation remains a headwind, particularly in auto repairs at 12% and medical costs, but our 10.2% average rate increases in Personal Auto and pricing engines like UnityPrice 3.0 have more than offset it, keeping our ex-cat loss ratios stable and supporting premium growth.

Operator: Our next question comes from Taylor Brooks with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Taylor Brooks: What is the expected impact of new IFRS 17 regulations on your underwriting strategy?

Lisa Patel: Good morning, Taylor. IFRS 17 enhances transparency on financial liabilities, and we've adapted by refining our CSM projections and risk adjustment methodologies. It supports our disciplined pricing, with minimal impact on strategy as our attritional combined ratio stays below 93%.

Operator: Our next question comes from Chris Patel with Barclays. Please go ahead.

Chris Patel: Thanks. On capital deployment, any updates on the APAC health micro-insurer deal?

Michael Chen: Chris, we're in exclusivity for that 51% stake, expecting to close in Q1 2025. It fits our growth in parametric health products amid the gig economy boom, funded without straining our 512% RBC.
